title: New police motorcycle camera team to target speeding across Thames Valley
summary: Thames Valley Police says a new motorcycle safety camera team will help officers reach speeding hotspots near schools, rural communities and roads where camera vans are harder to deploy.
body: A new police motorcycle camera team is being launched across Thames Valley as part of a wider push to reduce serious collisions and deaths on the region’s roads.

Thames Valley Police says the new Safety Camera Motorcyclist capability will allow trained camera operators to reach places where a traditional safety camera van may not be suitable, including areas near schools, rural communities and roads with limited space or access.

For residents in Witney and across West Oxfordshire, the change could be relevant where speeding concerns are raised on local routes, village roads and school-run approaches. The force says deployments will be guided by collision data, community concerns and local policing priorities.

body.text: How the new team will work

body: The motorcycles will be equipped with handheld laser and video speed detection technology. Police say this should make enforcement more flexible and allow officers to respond more quickly to areas where speeding or dangerous driving has been identified as a concern.
Local policing teams will also be able to raise issues reported in their communities. Where a genuine concern is identified, deployments can be made to provide targeted enforcement and reassurance.
The force says offences detected by the new team will be processed through existing procedures, with Notices of Intended Prosecution issued where appropriate.

The launch supports the force’s continued focus on the so-called Fatal Five offences: speeding, drink and drug driving, not wearing a seatbelt, using a mobile phone while driving, and careless or dangerous driving.

Those offences are treated as priorities because they are among the main behaviours linked to serious collisions. Thames Valley Police says the new team is intended to sit alongside education and engagement work, not replace it.

Superintendent Euan Livingstone, head of the Roads Policing Unit, said the force hears clear and consistent concern from communities about speeding and wants the new capability to show that those concerns are being acted on.

Thames Valley Police and Crime Commissioner Matthew Barber said the team would help officers reach areas where traditional camera vans cannot, strengthening enforcement against dangerous and illegal behaviour on the roads.

The announcement does not list specific Witney deployment sites. However, the ability to use smaller, mobile camera teams could matter in towns and villages where residents have long-standing concerns about speeding but where larger enforcement vehicles are difficult to position safely.
The capability is funded through the TVP Road Safety Fund, with joint oversight from Thames Valley Police and the Police and Crime Commissioner.

Source: Thames Valley Police. Image note: Witney Wire has not copied Thames Valley Police photographs without separate permission; this story uses an existing road-safety graphic from the Witney Wire site.

title: Criminal cash to fund phone-free schools as Oxford head’s approach gains backing
summary: Schools across the Thames Valley could receive funding to help keep pupils off mobile phones during the school day, as an Oxford school’s stricter approach attracts wider attention.
body: Schools across the Thames Valley could soon receive funding to help keep mobile phones out of classrooms, as a new initiative backed by the region’s Police and Crime Commissioner builds on an approach already championed by one of Oxford’s best-known headteachers.

The scheme, announced by Police and Crime Commissioner Matthew Barber, will use £255,000 of funding to support secondary schools in Berkshire, Buckinghamshire, Oxfordshire and Milton Keynes to become phone-free during the school day.

Schools will be able to apply for support towards practical measures such as secure storage, including lockable pouches, lockers or boxes, so pupils are unable to access their phones while lessons and school activities are taking place.

The funding is aimed at reducing disruption in classrooms, improving safeguarding and giving pupils a break from online pressures during the school day. According to the PCC, the money comes from criminals, including proceeds from the sale of stolen goods that cannot be returned and court orders made against offenders.

The announcement comes as attention continues to grow around Alastair Chirnside, Warden of St Edward’s School in Oxford, whose stricter phone policy has been credited with improving pupil wellbeing and school life. Mr Chirnside is also set to become Head Master of Eton College, bringing further attention to his approach.

At St Edward’s, younger pupils have faced significant limits on smartphone use during the school week, while the school has also brought back traditional landline telephones in boarding houses to encourage more direct conversations between pupils and their families.

The change has been praised for encouraging pupils to spend more time talking to each other, taking part in sport, reading, and becoming more involved in school activities rather than spending breaks and evenings on their phones.

The Police and Crime Commissioner’s new fund could allow more schools to introduce similar systems without having to meet the full cost themselves. Schools will be expected to use the funding for policies that prevent pupils from accessing and using their phones throughout the whole school day.

The issue has become part of a wider national debate about children’s smartphone use, with concerns raised about distraction, online bullying, peer pressure, harmful content and the effect of screen time on young people’s mental health.

For families and schools across Oxfordshire, the funding marks another step towards phone-free school days becoming more common, while the success of St Edward’s suggests the change can have benefits beyond the classroom.

Secondary schools, middle schools and all-through schools are eligible to apply for the funding, while primary schools, sixth form colleges and private schools are not included in the scheme. Applications are due to close on Sunday 26 July 2026.

title: Concerns raised over plans for asylum accommodation at MOD Bicester
summary: Plans to seek permission for asylum seeker accommodation at MOD Bicester have prompted calls for clearer information about policing, local services and community impact.
body: Plans to seek permission for asylum seeker accommodation at MOD Bicester have prompted calls for clearer information from national government about policing, community impact and local services.

The proposal follows a Home Office announcement that it is exploring the use of three Ministry of Defence sites, including one near Bicester, as part of wider plans to reduce the use of hotels for asylum accommodation.

Thames Valley Police and Crime Commissioner Matthew Barber said he had concerns about the possible impact on local policing, particularly if additional demand is placed on officers in and around the site.

In a statement, Mr Barber said he had not had direct communication from the Home Office about the plans before the announcement was made. He said he had written to the Home Secretary requesting a meeting to discuss what additional resources may be needed if the proposal goes ahead.

The site identified near Bicester is understood to be part of Bicester Garrison, located between Piddington and Upper Arncott. Local representatives have said they want more detail about the potential impact on residents, public services and community safety before any plans move forward.

The Home Office has said the use of former or existing military sites is part of its effort to reduce reliance on hotels. In the Thames Valley area, the PCC statement also referred to the expected closure of the Oxford Witney Hotel and the Mercure George Hotel in Reading as asylum hotels.

Supporters of moving away from hotel accommodation argue that the current system is expensive and has placed pressure on communities where hotels have been used for long periods. However, local representatives have said that any alternative sites must be properly planned, with clear information about security, safeguarding, healthcare, transport and policing.

The issue is likely to remain sensitive locally, with concerns about community impact needing to be balanced against the national challenge of providing accommodation for people while their asylum claims are processed.
No final decision has yet been reported, and the proposal would still need to go through the relevant planning and approval processes.

For residents in Bicester and the wider Oxfordshire area, the key questions are now likely to focus on how many people could be accommodated, when any site might open, what services would be required, and whether additional funding would be provided to support local policing and public services.
Local councils, police representatives and residents are expected to seek further information from the Home Office before the plans move forward.
Source: Thames Valley Police and Crime Commissioner statement on planned asylum accommodation at MOD Bicester.

title: Summer days out for children near Witney: four local ideas for the holidays
summary: From Oxford’s museums to Blenheim Palace, Millets Farm and the ruins at Minster Lovell, here are family days out within reach of Witney this summer.
body: Families looking for things to do with children over the summer do not have to travel far from Witney to find a good day out.
From Oxford’s museums to palace gardens, farm attractions and riverside ruins, there are several places within easy reach that offer a mix of learning, fresh air and family-friendly exploring.
Here are four ideas for summer days out in and around Oxfordshire.

body.alt: Families walking towards Oxford museum buildings on a sunny day
body.caption: AI-generated illustration: Families visiting Oxford’s museums during the summer holidays.

body: Oxford is one of the easiest places to turn a wet or uncertain summer day into something memorable.

The city’s museums offer plenty for children, especially families who want something educational without it feeling too much like school. The Oxford University Museum of Natural History runs family-friendly events and activities, while the Pitt Rivers Museum offers family trails, crafts and activities for children.
The Ashmolean Museum is another option for families, with art, archaeology, family trails, Explorer packs and interactive resources designed to help younger visitors explore the collections.

Families could also consider The Story Museum in Oxford, which is built around books, storytelling and imaginative play. Its spaces include the Galleries, recommended for ages five and over, and Small Worlds, a story-play area aimed at younger children. The museum is also listing Great British Summer Savings prices for this summer, including reduced child ticket prices, so families should check the official booking page before travelling.

For Witney families, Oxford’s museums are a useful summer option because they work well in different weather and can be combined with lunch, a walk through the city or a short visit to the Covered Market.

body.alt: Families enjoying outdoor play near Blenheim Palace
body.caption: AI-generated illustration: Families enjoying a summer day out at Blenheim Palace.

body.text: Make a day of it at Blenheim Palace

body: Blenheim Palace remains one of Oxfordshire’s biggest family days out, particularly during the school holidays.

The palace grounds offer space to walk, explore and picnic, while Adventure Play gives children a dedicated area to climb, slide, splash and burn off energy. Blenheim describes the play area as a place where children can explore tunnels, bridges, cargo nets, hidden chambers, slides and water play.
Blenheim is also a useful option for mixed-age groups, as adults can enjoy the gardens, views and palace setting while children have space to play and explore.
As with many larger attractions, it is worth checking ticket options and opening times before travelling, particularly during busy summer dates.

body.alt: Families at an outdoor farm play area on a sunny day
body.caption: AI-generated illustration: A family summer day out at a farm attraction.

body: Millets Farm, near Frilford, is another reliable family option within reach of Witney.

The site promotes a mix of things to do, including family attractions, shopping, places to eat and seasonal events. Its outdoor play area is free to enter, while Sprouts Play Barn offers an indoor soft play option, including a dedicated area for under-fives.

For younger children, the appeal is often simple: animals, space to move around, food, treats and things to explore. For parents, the benefit is that there is enough on site to make the trip feel easy and flexible.
Families should check ahead for which activities are free, which need booking and whether any special summer events are running.

body.alt: Family walking beside riverside ruins at Minster Lovell
body.caption: AI-generated illustration: Families exploring the ruins at Minster Lovell.

body: For a quieter and more local option, Minster Lovell Hall and Dovecote offers a very different kind of day out.

The ruins sit beside the River Windrush and give children the chance to explore a piece of local history in the open air. English Heritage describes the site as the picturesque ruins of a 15th-century Oxfordshire manor house, including a hall, tower and nearby dovecote.

For families who enjoy walks, picnics, history or photography, Minster Lovell can make a gentle summer outing close to Witney. Children can imagine what the old manor house might once have looked like, while adults can enjoy the peaceful riverside setting.
It is a good reminder that not every summer day out needs to be expensive or heavily planned. Sometimes a short local trip, a packed lunch and a bit of imagination are enough.
Opening times, ticket prices and activities can change during the summer, so families should check official websites before setting off.

For many parents, the best summer days out are the ones that balance cost, travel time and flexibility. Oxford’s museums, The Story Museum, Blenheim Palace, Millets Farm and Minster Lovell all offer something different — whether families want learning, play, animals, history or simply a reason to get out of the house.
And for children growing up around Witney, these local trips can become the kind of summer memories that last long after the holidays are over.
Sources: Oxford University Museum of Natural History, Pitt Rivers Museum, Ashmolean Museum, The Story Museum, Blenheim Palace, Millets Farm Centre and English Heritage.

title: M40 drivers warned as five sets of roadworks planned over busy weekend
summary: Drivers using the M40 through Oxfordshire are being urged to plan ahead, with several overnight and daytime roadworks scheduled between Friday 27 June and Monday 30 June 2026.
body: Drivers using the M40 through Oxfordshire are being urged to plan ahead after National Highways confirmed a series of planned roadworks affecting both northbound and southbound traffic over the coming days.

Most of the disruption is expected to take place on the evening of Friday 27 June through to the morning of Saturday 28 June, with additional overnight works scheduled between Sunday 29 June and Monday 30 June.

The first planned works begin at 9pm on Friday 27 June, when two of the three southbound lanes will close between junctions 11 and 10. The restrictions will remain in place until 6am on Saturday 28 June.
At the same time, a separate section of the M40 southbound between junctions 10 and 9 will also have lanes one and two closed overnight, with the same 9pm to 6am schedule.

Further south, motorists travelling towards London will face more significant restrictions between junctions 2 and 1A, where three of the four southbound lanes are due to close from 9pm on Friday until 6am on Saturday while planned roadworks are carried out.
Drivers should also be aware of emergency roadworks between junctions 16 and 15 southbound, where disruption is expected between 8am and 6pm on both Friday 27 and Saturday 28 June.
A separate scheme will then affect the M40 northbound between junctions 10 and 12, where overnight roadworks are scheduled from 8pm on Sunday 29 June until 6am on Monday 30 June.

Planned M40 roadworks: Friday 27 June to Saturday 28 June — J11 to J10 southbound: lanes 1 and 2 closed from 9pm to 6am; J10 to J9 southbound: lanes 1 and 2 closed from 9pm to 6am; J2 to J1A southbound: lanes 1, 2 and 3 closed from 9pm to 6am; J16 to J15 southbound: emergency roadworks with disruption expected between 8am and 6pm on both days.
Planned M40 roadworks: Sunday 29 June to Monday 30 June — J10 to J12 northbound: planned overnight roadworks from 8pm until 6am.

Motorists travelling between Oxfordshire, Warwickshire, Buckinghamshire and London are advised to allow extra time for their journeys, particularly during overnight periods when lane closures are in place. Road users should follow signed diversions where applicable and take extra care when travelling through roadwork zones.
As with all planned motorway works, schedules can change at short notice, so drivers are encouraged to check the latest traffic information before setting off.

title: Global electric vehicle company opens new engineering hub in Witney
summary: NIO has opened a new engineering and research facility in Witney, bringing together more than 40 specialist engineers and strengthening Oxfordshire’s role in electric vehicle innovation.
body: A leading global electric vehicle manufacturer has strengthened its commitment to Oxfordshire after opening a new engineering and research facility in Witney, bringing together more than 40 specialist engineers under one roof.
NIO, one of the world’s fastest-growing smart electric vehicle companies, officially opened its new engineering hub as it celebrated 10 years of research and development in the UK.

The new facility consolidates the company’s previous engineering operations into a single base in Witney, creating a central location for advanced vehicle engineering, computer-aided engineering, testing and technology development.
Company leaders say the move reflects NIO’s long-term commitment to the UK and reinforces Oxfordshire’s reputation as one of Europe’s leading centres for automotive engineering and innovation.

The Witney team has played a significant role in developing some of NIO’s most advanced electric vehicles over the past decade, including work on vehicle dynamics, engineering validation and chassis development.
Engineers based in Oxfordshire have also contributed to the company’s EP9 electric supercar and more recent production models sold across international markets.

The new engineering centre spans approximately 9,460 square feet and combines virtual engineering specialists with physical testing facilities. NIO says the expanded site will allow its UK engineers to work even more closely with teams across Europe and China as the company develops future generations of smart electric vehicles.

Hui Zhang, Vice President of NIO Europe, said the Oxfordshire team has become an integral part of the company’s global research and development network over the past decade, contributing to multiple vehicle programmes and engineering innovations.

For Witney, the investment represents another boost for the town’s growing reputation in high-value engineering and technology. Oxfordshire is already home to internationally recognised automotive businesses, Formula One engineering companies and advanced manufacturing organisations, making the county one of the UK’s leading centres for transport innovation.

While many residents will know Witney for its independent businesses and town centre trade, the arrival of a larger engineering operation also highlights the town’s role in attracting international investment and creating highly skilled employment opportunities.

As demand for electric vehicles and sustainable transport technologies continues to grow worldwide, companies such as NIO are increasingly investing in research, engineering and software development to remain competitive.

For local residents considering careers in engineering, software, automotive technology or advanced manufacturing, the continued investment by global companies provides another reminder that internationally recognised opportunities are being created on Witney’s doorstep.
Sources: NIO announcement and industry reporting by The EV Report on the opening of the new Witney engineering facility.
author: Robert

title: Could the next England star come from Witney?
summary: As World Cup excitement builds, local grassroots clubs in Witney could see more young players inspired to pull on their boots.
body: As England’s World Cup campaign captures attention across the country, football clubs in and around Witney could be set for a fresh wave of interest from children inspired by the tournament.

Major international competitions have a way of turning living rooms into mini stadiums, with young fans copying goals, saves and celebrations in gardens, parks and playgrounds the next day. For local clubs, that excitement can be the spark that encourages a child to join a team for the first time.

In Witney, grassroots football is already supported by clubs offering opportunities across a range of ages and abilities. Witney Vikings Youth Football Club says it was established in 1975, has more than 40 teams, and describes itself as the largest youth football club in the Witney area. Source: Witney Vikings Youth Football Club.

Tower Hill Football Club, also based in Witney, says it is an England Football accredited club with youth teams from under-six to under-18 level, as well as women’s, men’s and inclusive teams. The club says its mission is to provide competitive football locally in a safe and controlled environment under FA-qualified coaches. Source: Tower Hill Football Club.

The local picture matters because grassroots football is often where children first learn more than how to pass, shoot or tackle. For many young players, the game helps build confidence, teamwork, discipline and friendships that last well beyond the final whistle.

England Football, the Football Association’s participation platform, encourages families to find local youth football opportunities, including mini-soccer, 9-a-side and 11-a-side football. It also highlights programmes such as Wildcats, aimed at girls aged five to 11, and Comets, a pan-disability football programme for disabled children aged five to 11. Source: England Football.

That wider national push could be important locally if the World Cup encourages more children in Witney to get involved. Clubs depend not only on players, but also on parents, coaches, helpers and volunteers who give up evenings and weekends to keep grassroots football running.

The tournament also offers a reminder that football is not only for children already dreaming of playing for England. Many clubs now provide routes for beginners, girls, boys, disabled children and players who simply want to enjoy being part of a team.
For parents, the message is simple: if the World Cup has sparked an interest, now could be a good time to look at what is available locally.

Whether or not the next England star comes from Witney, the tournament could still leave a lasting legacy if it encourages more children to pull on their boots, join a club and enjoy the game with friends.
For many young players, the journey does not begin in a stadium. It starts on a local pitch, with a volunteer coach, a pair of shin pads and a Saturday morning kick-off.
Sources: Witney Vikings Youth Football Club; Tower Hill Football Club; England Football.
author: Mark

title: Why M&S Café in Witney Might Be the Best Spot in Town for a Coffee Break
summary: From consistently hot coffee to friendly staff and a relaxed atmosphere, the M&S Café in Witney has quietly become one of the town’s most reliable places to stop and recharge.
body: There are plenty of places to grab a coffee in Witney, but the M&S Café inside Marks & Spencer continues to stand out for all the right reasons.
In a time where service can often feel rushed or inconsistent, the café manages to keep things simple: good coffee, friendly staff and a genuinely pleasant atmosphere.
One thing that always stands out is that the coffee is actually hot when it arrives — something that surprisingly isn’t guaranteed everywhere these days.
Whether stopping in for a quick drink while shopping or taking a short break during the day, the café consistently delivers a reliable experience.
The service is also worth mentioning. Staff are regularly welcoming, polite and patient, even during busier periods, which makes the whole place feel far more relaxed than many chain cafés.
The café itself is clean, comfortable and usually calm enough to sit for a while without feeling hurried out the door.
While independent cafés will always play an important role in Witney’s town centre, the M&S Café deserves credit for quietly doing the basics very well — and doing them consistently.
Sometimes that’s exactly what people are looking for.

summary: Drivers are being advised to plan ahead, with several M40 lane closures, slip-road works and horticultural works scheduled from 28 June into early July.
body: Drivers using the M40 are being advised to plan ahead, with a series of planned roadworks, barrier repairs and lane closures affecting several stretches of the motorway from Sunday 28 June.
The earliest listed works affect the M40 northbound between junctions 1A and 2, where horticultural works are scheduled from 7am on Sunday 28 June until 11.59pm on Monday 29 June.

A separate notice has also been issued for the same northbound stretch between junctions 1A and 2, again for horticultural works, with a later schedule running from 7pm on Sunday 28 June until 11.59pm on Friday 3 July. Drivers are advised to check live traffic information before travelling, as multiple notices are currently listed for this section.
From 9pm on Sunday 28 June until 6am on Monday 29 June, lane three is due to close on the M40 northbound between junctions 10 and 11 for planned barrier repairs.

During the same overnight period, lanes two and three are scheduled to close on the M40 southbound between junctions 11 and 10, also for barrier repairs. Two of the three lanes are expected to be closed.

Later that evening, further disruption is planned around junction 4 northbound. The northbound exit slip at junction 4 is scheduled to close from 10.15pm on Sunday 28 June until 6am on Monday 29 June, with all lanes closed while roadworks take place.

Also from 10.15pm to 6am, lanes one and two are due to close on the M40 northbound between junctions 3 and 4, while a separate notice for the M40 northbound within junction 4 states that lanes one and two will be closed and all lanes at the junction will be affected during the same overnight works.

In date order, the main listed works are: J1A to J2 northbound horticultural works from 7am on 28 June to 11.59pm on 29 June; J1A to J2 northbound horticultural works from 7pm on 28 June to 11.59pm on 3 July; J10 to J11 northbound lane three closure for barrier repairs from 9pm on 28 June to 6am on 29 June; J11 to J10 southbound lanes two and three closed for barrier repairs from 9pm on 28 June to 6am on 29 June; J4 northbound exit slip closed from 10.15pm on 28 June to 6am on 29 June; J3 to J4 northbound lanes one and two closed from 10.15pm on 28 June to 6am on 29 June; and northbound works within junction 4 from 10.15pm on 28 June to 6am on 29 June.

Motorists travelling through Oxfordshire, Buckinghamshire and towards London or Birmingham should allow extra time, particularly on Sunday evening and overnight into Monday morning when several closures are scheduled at once.
As with all planned roadworks, timings can change at short notice, so drivers are encouraged to check the latest travel information before setting off.

title: Oxford man jailed after police witness drug deal in city park
summary: Craig Ballantyne has been jailed after Thames Valley Police officers saw a drug deal in Oxford and later found him in possession of crack cocaine.
body: An Oxford man has been jailed after police officers witnessed a drug deal in the city and later found him in possession of crack cocaine.
Craig Ballantyne, 38, of Burton Place, Oxford, was sentenced at Oxford Crown Court on Thursday 25 June to two years and six months in prison.
Thames Valley Police said Ballantyne had previously pleaded guilty to one count of possession with intent to supply class A drugs, namely crack cocaine, at a hearing on 29 May.
The case followed an incident in Frys Hill Park, Oxford, on 28 April this year. Police said Ballantyne was stopped by plain-clothed officers after they witnessed a drug deal taking place.
Following the stop, Ballantyne was found in possession of crack cocaine. Thames Valley Police said testing later confirmed the substance.
For readers across Oxfordshire, the case is part of the force’s continued work targeting class A drug supply and the harm linked to drug-related crime in local communities.
Investigating officer PC Daniel Cook said Ballantyne had shown a blatant disregard for the law by returning to class A drug supply shortly after being released from prison.
He said the swift arrest and conviction demonstrated the force’s continued commitment to tackling drug-related crime and protecting communities from repeat offending.
Source and image: Thames Valley Police.
author: Witney Wire Newsdesk

title: Police AI assistant Bobbi helps thousands access support in first six months
summary: Thames Valley Police says its AI assistant Bobbi is helping people get advice and support more quickly while freeing staff to focus on urgent and complex cases.
body: An AI virtual assistant used by Thames Valley Police is helping thousands of people access support more quickly, six months after it was launched.

Bobbi, which is used by Thames Valley Police and Hampshire & Isle of Wight Constabulary, was introduced in November 2025 as an extra way for the public to ask questions, seek advice and get help with non-emergency enquiries.

The force says Bobbi is not there to replace officers or staff. Instead, it works alongside online forms and telephone lines, giving people another option when they need guidance or want to report a concern.
According to Thames Valley Police, Bobbi has handled around 200 non-emergency conversations a day in its first six months, with about 45 per cent fully resolved without staff intervention.

The force says that is the equivalent of supporting around 14,000 public contacts a year while freeing more than 3,200 hours for contact centre staff, allowing them to spend more time on emergencies and sensitive cases.

Police also say the assistant is helping to identify risk earlier. Since launch, Bobbi has identified at least one high-harm offence every day requiring escalation to a Digital Desk operator, with an average of two cases involving violence against women and girls detected daily for immediate intervention.

body.text: A wider positive role for AI

body: For communities across Oxfordshire, including Witney and West Oxfordshire, the development is another example of how AI can have a positive impact when it is used carefully and responsibly. It can make public services easier to access, reduce delays for routine enquiries and help human staff focus on the situations where they are needed most.

Thames Valley Police says one of Bobbi's biggest strengths is accessibility. The service is available 24 hours a day, provides a discreet way to seek help when speaking on the phone may not be possible, and can support multiple languages.

In one case highlighted by the force, a young person was able to discreetly seek advice about a high-risk domestic incident via Bobbi when it was not safe to speak aloud. The assistant detected the risk, escalated the case and enabled a handover to a live operator who dispatched officers.

The force says Bobbi is built using information supplied by Thames Valley Police and Hampshire & Isle of Wight Constabulary, and that data shared during chats remains confidential and is not used outside the two forces.
Further development is already under way, with contact centre supervisors continuing to train the system so it stays up to date with legislation and policies.
Source: Thames Valley Police. Image: AI-generated illustration for Witney Wire.
author: Robert

title: Tractors took to the roads in Witney for charity road run
summary: Vintage, classic and modern tractors travelled through Witney as part of a community road run raising money for Antics Charity, which supports children affected by cancer.
body: Tractors took to the roads in Witney for a charity road run in support of children affected by cancer.
The Witney Tractor Road Run brought together tractor owners, supporters and local residents for a day of community fundraising.
The event was held in aid of Antics Charity, which helps children affected by cancer, and welcomed a mix of vintage, classic and modern tractors.
Photos taken by Witney Wire showed tractors travelling through Witney, with large agricultural vehicles drawing attention from passing motorists and residents as they made their way through the town.
Gates opened at 8.30am, with tractors departing at 10.30am.
The entry fee was £20 per tractor, and organisers had encouraged anyone with a vintage, classic or modern tractor to take part.
A BBQ and refreshments were also available during the day, giving families and spectators the chance to enjoy the atmosphere while supporting a good cause.
The road run brought together countryside tradition, local community spirit and fundraising, while helping to raise awareness and support for Antics Charity.
Images: Witney Wire.
author: Witney Wire Newsdesk

title: Police investigation into Bicester Motion fire deaths handed to HSE
summary: Thames Valley Police says it has completed its investigation into the deaths of three people following the fire at Bicester Motion last year, with the Health and Safety Executive now leading the next stage.
body: Thames Valley Police has completed its investigation into the deaths of three people following the fire at Bicester Motion last year.
Firefighters Martyn Sadler and Jennie Logan, along with member of the public Dave Chester, died after the fire at the business park on Buckingham Road, Bicester, on 15 May 2025.
Two other firefighters were also seriously injured.
Police said their Major Crime Unit had carried out a thorough investigation alongside the Health and Safety Executive.
The force has confirmed it has not made any referrals to the Crown Prosecution Service for charging decisions.
A file is now being prepared for the coroner, and police say they will support the forthcoming inquest.
Assistant Chief Constable Dennis Murray said the force’s thoughts remained with the loved ones of Martyn Sadler, Jennie Logan and Dave Chester, as well as the firefighters who were injured.
He said the police investigation into the tragic incident had now been completed and that the force was not seeking any prosecutions.
The investigation has now formally been handed to the Health and Safety Executive, which will lead the next stage of enquiries into the circumstances of what happened.
An HSE spokesperson said it was now leading the investigation.
Image: Witney Wire.
author: Witney Wire Newsdesk

title: Two sentenced over Class A drug supply in Oxford
summary: Two people have been sentenced after a Thames Valley Police investigation uncovered class A drugs, mobile phones and dealing paraphernalia in Oxford.
body: Two people have been sentenced following a Thames Valley Police investigation into the supply of class A drugs in Oxford.
Cameron Riordan, 27, of Reedmace Close, Blackbird Leys, was sentenced at Oxford Crown Court on Friday 14 August to four years and eight months in prison.

Charley Webb, 29, of Pottery Place, Blackbird Leys, was given a sentence of one year and eight months, suspended for two years. She must also complete a 15-day rehabilitation requirement and pay £187 in costs.
Riordan pleaded guilty to offences including possession with intent to supply cocaine, heroin and crack cocaine, along with being concerned in the supply of heroin and crack cocaine.
Webb pleaded guilty to being concerned in the supply of heroin and cocaine.

Police said officers arrested Riordan on 16 February after receiving information that he was operating a drugs line in Oxford. During a search, officers recovered heroin, crack cocaine and two mobile phones.
Analysis of one of the devices later indicated that drugs were being stored at Webb's address in exchange for cash payments.
Officers searched Webb's address on 19 February and recovered a safe containing crack cocaine, heroin and cocaine with an estimated street value of £9,980.
Additional mobile phones and drug supply paraphernalia were also seized, including scales, blades and deal bags used for packaging controlled drugs.
Thames Valley Police said the case formed part of its continued work to disrupt drug supply networks and prevent harmful class A drugs from reaching local communities.
Source: Thames Valley Police.
author: Mary

title: Long-term transport plan approved for Witney and Carterton
summary: Oxfordshire County Council has approved a 25-year strategy for transport in Witney, Carterton and neighbouring communities, setting out ambitions for buses, walking and cycling.
author: Witney Wire Newsdesk
body: A long-term transport strategy aimed at improving connections across Witney, Carterton and surrounding communities has been approved by Oxfordshire County Council.
The West Oxfordshire Lowlands Movement and Place Plan sets out a 25-year approach to transport across the area, with 15 objectives and 114 supporting actions.

The plan focuses on improving opportunities for walking, cycling, wheeling and public transport, while recognising that private vehicles will remain necessary for some residents, particularly in rural communities.
Among the priorities are more reliable and integrated bus services, better pedestrian and cycling connections, and transport hubs designed to make journeys between different services easier.
The strategy also supports work to improve rail connections and follows ongoing consideration of rapid transit options between the Witney area and Oxford.
The council says approximately 87,000 people live in the West Oxfordshire Lowlands area, with around 16% commuting to Oxford for work.

The newly approved plan will help guide future transport projects and support efforts to secure funding. However, approval of the strategy does not mean that every proposed improvement has received construction funding or a confirmed delivery date.
For communities that rely heavily on road transport, the key question will be how quickly the long-term ambitions translate into practical improvements.

title: Witney market wins strong backing from shoppers in council survey
summary: A council survey reports high customer satisfaction at Witney's Charter Market, with the operator's first year also seeing strong stall occupancy.
author: Witney Wire Newsdesk
body: Witney's Charter Market has received encouraging feedback from shoppers following changes to the management of local markets.

A survey published by West Oxfordshire District Council found that 98% of 143 customers questioned were satisfied with customer service, while 96% were satisfied with product quality and 95% with the market atmosphere.
The results follow the first year of operations under Cotswold Markets Ltd, which took over the management of Witney and Chipping Norton's Charter Markets in August 2025.
According to the council, stall occupancy at Witney has regularly reached between 90% and 99%, exceeding the council's 75% target.
The council's Executive has supported extending the agreement with the operator following its review of the first year.
The findings also suggest improvements in market organisation, stall variety and trader confidence, although traders identified a continuing need to attract more visitors and raise awareness.
Markets remain an important part of Witney town centre, supporting independent businesses and offering residents an alternative to larger retail outlets.
The council and market operator say their next priorities include attracting additional traders, improving signage and exploring more activities to encourage visits.
The satisfaction figures reflect the views of those surveyed and should not be interpreted as representing every shopper.

title: Free Halloween fun comes to Marriotts Walk this half term
summary: Families can take part in a free Pumpkin Trail and Pumpkin Patch at Marriotts Walk in Witney during October half term, from 26 to 31 October.
author: Witney Wire Newsdesk
body: Families looking for something to do during the October half-term holiday can enjoy free Halloween-themed activities at Marriotts Walk in Witney.
The shopping centre is hosting a Pumpkin Trail and a pop-up Pumpkin Patch from Monday 26 October until Saturday 31 October.
The activities are designed to give younger visitors something seasonal to enjoy while encouraging families to spend time in Witney town centre.
The Pumpkin Trail offers an opportunity to explore the shopping centre, while the Pumpkin Patch provides a themed setting for family photographs.
West Oxfordshire District Council says the activities form part of efforts to support town-centre businesses and attract more visitors.

The council also reported that footfall at Marriotts Walk had increased by 23.7% year on year, although that figure should be treated as a reported measure rather than evidence that this week's event caused the increase.
Both activities are advertised as free, making them an option for families looking for a half-term outing without an admission charge.
Visitors should check the event organiser's latest information for participation arrangements and opening times before travelling.
